solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Short, giant, bizarre funfair attraction (5,5)

indicators.note: a bizarre arrangement of letters is a jumbled one

annotation.surface: A fairground ride sized up as a tiny giant, which is bizarre indeed.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Short' and 'giant' look like a contradiction to puzzle over; they are simply the ten letters to rearrange.
annotation.definitionFit: A ghost train is the dark fairground ride full of spooks.

clue.text: Chat about queen’s dress (4)

indicators.note: one piece goes about, i.e. around, the other

annotation.surface: Gossip about what the queen is wearing.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Chat about' reads as gossip on a subject; 'about' is the instruction to wrap, and the queen is the usual Regina abbreviation.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both words mean clothing, the first the more old-fashioned term.

clue.text: Periodical in charge of Nature (7)

definitions.note: Nature is a noun used attributively here; ORGANIC is the adjective 'of nature'

blocks.note: an organ is a newspaper or journal of a party or group

annotation.surface: A magazine editor who runs the science journal Nature.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Nature' is capitalised to look like the journal, which suits the periodical; it is the definition, with ORGANIC meaning natural.
annotation.definitionFit: Organic things come from nature rather than the laboratory.

clue.text: Article on extremely flagrant crime (5)

indicators.note: take the extremes, first and last letters

blocks.note: the outer letters of FlagranT; 'on' places THE first

annotation.surface: A newspaper piece about a blatant offence.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Article' looks like a newspaper story, which suits the crime; it is the grammar word THE.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: stealing is one particular kind of crime.

clue.text: Hired guards seen occasionally felt bitter (8)

indicators.note: RENTED guards, i.e. holds, the other piece
take the letters on occasion, every other one

annotation.surface: Security guards on a contract, only seen now and then, left the client sour.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Hired guards' reads as hired security staff; 'guards' is really the container instruction, and 'occasionally' takes every other letter.
annotation.definitionFit: To resent something is to feel bitter about it.

clue.text: State what to say at the altar about a husband (5)

indicators.note: I DO goes about, i.e. around, A H

blocks.clueFragment: what to say at the altar

annotation.surface: A wedding: what the bride says, turning towards her husband.
annotation.walkthrough: 'State' opens the clue looking like the verb 'say'; it is the US state, and the wedding vow wraps round A H.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: the Gem State in the American north-west is one of the fifty US states.

clue.text: Begin to wake in prison (4)

blocks.note: to rouse from sleep and start moving

annotation.surface: A prisoner coming round in the cell one morning.
annotation.walkthrough: Two meanings of one word, joined by 'in': to stir, and the stir, old slang for jail.
annotation.definitionFit: You stir as you start to wake; 'in stir' means in jail.

clue.text: Unimportant court case imprisoning four (7)

indicators.note: to imprison is to hold inside, so TRIAL holds IV within it

blocks.note: a trial is a court case

annotation.surface: A minor court case where four people end up behind bars.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Imprisoning' suits the courtroom scene, but here it only means one piece holds the other, and the four is a Roman numeral.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both describe something too slight to matter.

clue.text: Feeling sorry about river bird with metal leg in the end (10)

indicators.note: take the end of 'leg', its last letter

blocks.note: an egret is a white heron

annotation.surface: Pity for a wading bird fitted with a metal prosthetic leg.
annotation.walkthrough: The bird with a metal leg is a sad little scene, which hides a plain string of pieces: R, EGRET, TIN and the last letter of 'leg'.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to rue something and to feel sorry about it are the same state of mind.

clue.text: Most severe back issue resists treatment ultimately (8)

indicators.note: take the ultimate, last, letter of each word

blocks.note: the stern is the back of a ship
the last letters of issuE resistS treatmenT

annotation.surface: A patient's worst back problem that won't respond to any therapy.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Back issue' reads as a medical complaint; 'back' alone is STERN, and 'issue' belongs to the run of last letters.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in superlative form: stern and severe both mean strict and harsh.

clue.text: Scoundrel with Irish accent losing face (5)

indicators.note: a word's face is its front, the first letter, which goes

blocks.note: BROGUE, an Irish accent, without its first letter B

annotation.surface: A rascal with an Irish lilt being humiliated.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Losing face' looks like embarrassment, which fits a scoundrel; here it removes the front letter of BROGUE.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both words name a dishonest rascal.

clue.text: Dramatic beginning to grip learner (9)

indicators.note: STARTING grips, holds, the L

annotation.surface: A theatrical start to a learner's driving lesson.
annotation.walkthrough: START(L)ING. 'Beginning' tempts you to take a first letter; it is the whole word STARTING, with L slipped in.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both describe something that makes you jump with surprise.

clue.text: Union flyer too rambling? Never! (3,2,4,4)

indicators.note: rambling letters wander out of order

annotation.surface: Asked whether a trade-union leaflet is too long-winded, someone flatly refuses.
annotation.walkthrough: The question mark turns the surface into a query and the answer into the retort to it.
annotation.definitionFit: 'Not on your life!' is an emphatic refusal, never.

clue.text: Hackneyed letters from Elizabeth read, bar endings (10)

indicators.note: the answer is made of consecutive letters taken from the words that follow

blocks.note: hidden in ElizabeTH READ, BAR Endings

annotation.surface: Stale old correspondence from Elizabeth, read out without its closing lines.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Bar endings' looks like an instruction to drop last letters; it is simply where the hidden answer finishes.
annotation.definitionFit: Threadbare, worn thin, is used of an overused, hackneyed idea.

clue.text: That man on vacation caught Oscar looking embarrassed and tormented (8)

indicators.note: a vacated word is emptied, keeping only its outer letters

annotation.surface: A holidaymaker caught with Oscar, red-faced and suffering for it.
annotation.walkthrough: 'That man on vacation' reads as one holidaying man; 'on vacation' actually empties 'caught' to CT.
annotation.definitionFit: To hector is to bully and torment.

clue.text: Renovated house not surpassed (8)

indicators.note: a renovated house is rebuilt, its letters remade

annotation.surface: A done-up house that still isn't beaten by any on the street.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Not surpassed' reads as a phrase; 'not' belongs to the fodder and 'surpassed' alone is the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to shine brighter than a rival is to surpass them, and both are past tense.

clue.text: On reflection, somewhat extol remarkable wine (6)

indicators.note: reflected letters run back to front
only some of the letters are used

annotation.surface: Thinking it over, a critic praises a fine wine, with some restraint.
annotation.walkthrough: 'On reflection' looks like 'after thinking it over'; it tells you to read the hidden letters backwards.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: the Bordeaux red grape gives its name to one of the world's most popular wines.

clue.text: Nurse with cracked lips, at first, damaged bit of hair (5,3)

indicators.note: cracked letters are broken up and rearranged
the lips' letters come first, before TEND

annotation.surface: A nurse with chapped lips and bad hair.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Nurse' comes first in the clue but its TEND goes last: 'at first' puts the cracked lips at the front.
annotation.definitionFit: A split end is a hair whose tip has frayed apart.

clue.text: Insists upon laws following English vote (6)

indicators.note: 'following' means coming after, so ACTS is placed after E and X

blocks.note: the cross on a ballot paper

annotation.surface: Someone demanding that laws follow a vote in England.
annotation.walkthrough: Assemble E and X first, then ACTS 'following' them.
annotation.definitionFit: To exact something is to insist on it, demand it.

clue.text: Trembling, answer first couple of questions – this person’s right (7)

indicators.note: a couple is two, so the first couple of a word are its first two letters

blocks.note: the first two letters of QUestions

annotation.surface: A nervous quiz contestant getting the first two questions right.
annotation.walkthrough: 'This person's' is the setter's I plus 's = has, giving I'VE, not a possessive.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a literary word for shaking with emotion.

clue.text: Doctor points to somewhere you can expectorate (8)

indicators.note: to doctor is to tamper with, rearrange

annotation.surface: A physician pointing a coughing patient to where they can spit.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Doctor' looks like the physician in a scene about expectorating; it is the verb meaning to tamper.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by description: the brass bowl once found in pubs and saloons was there for spitting into.

clue.text: Where hospital patients might be found at a point ahead (7)

definitions.text: Where hospital patients might be found

blocks.clueFragment: Where hospital patients might be found
blocks.note: patients lie in the long rooms of beds a hospital is divided into
forward, further along from a point in time or place

annotation.surface: Directions to the patients in a hospital, somewhere further along the corridor.
annotation.walkthrough: The first meaning needs the word split: patients are ON WARDS.
annotation.definitionFit: Double definition: patients lie in hospital wards, and the adverb means forward from a given point.

clue.text: Surprisingly win draught ale for relative (8-2-3)

indicators.note: the letters come out in a surprising order

annotation.surface: An unexpected pub raffle prize: beer on tap for a family member.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Draught' and 'daughter' share most of their letters, which is the setter's starting point; only W, I, N, L and E are added.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: a son's wife is one kind of relative, by marriage.

clue.text: Drug cheat with love for inspirational woman (5)

blocks.note: to rat is to betray or cheat

annotation.surface: A doping athlete in love with a woman who inspires them.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Drug cheat' reads as one sporting villain; it is two pieces, E and RAT.
annotation.definitionFit: Erato is the Muse of love poetry, and the Muses inspire artists.

clue.text: Big canal boat having left for capital of Bahrain (5)

indicators.note: L (left) takes the place of the named letter

blocks.note: a barge is a canal boat
the first letter of Bahrain, swapped out

annotation.surface: A huge boat that has departed for the Gulf state's capital.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Capital of Bahrain' tempts you to think of Manama; it is just its capital letter, B.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both describe something of great size.

clue.text: Most of aircraft blueprint (4)

indicators.note: 'most of' a word is nearly all of it, so its last letter is dropped

annotation.surface: Nearly the whole design drawing of an aeroplane.
annotation.walkthrough: The blueprint of an aircraft sounds like one thing; 'aircraft' only supplies PLANE.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: an architect's blueprint is the design or scheme for a building.

clue.text: Notice vehicle regularly that goes for profit (9)

indicators.note: take letters at regular intervals, every other one

blocks.note: the odd letters of ThAt GoEs

annotation.surface: Spotting a van that is regularly used as a money-maker.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Vehicle regularly' reads as a van in constant use; 'regularly' actually works on the next two words.
annotation.definitionFit: Advantage is profit or benefit, as in 'to your advantage'.

clue.text: Country right next to Russian river (5)

indicators.note: 'next to' means beside, so R is placed immediately before URAL

annotation.surface: A nation lying beside a river in Russia.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Country' looks like a nation, the obvious partner for a river; it is the adjective, as in country life.
annotation.definitionFit: Country and rural both describe the countryside.

clue.text: Nobleman contracted ahead of time (4)

indicators.note: shortened, losing its last letter

annotation.surface: An aristocrat who signed his contract early.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Contracted' looks like signing a deal; it means shortened, applied to EARLY.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: the British peer ranking between viscount and marquess is one kind of nobleman.

clue.text: Left Londoners worried for military hero (4,6)

indicators.note: worried letters are fretted into a new order

annotation.surface: Anxious Londoners left waiting for a hero to save them.
annotation.walkthrough: Nelson is the admiral who won Trafalgar, commemorated by Nelson's Column in London, which suits the Londoners.
annotation.definitionFit: Lord Nelson was Britain's great naval hero.
